prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT delay empiric antimicrobial therapy while awaiting imaging or LP results when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.

Do not perform lumbar puncture before cranial imaging in this patient: a severe immunocompromised state (post-traumatic asplenia with incomplete pneumococcal immunisation) is an imaging-first criterion under WHO 2025 section A.4.
Do NOT rely on a negative Gram stain or a 'normal CT' to rule out bacterial meningitis when the clinical syndrome is present.
Do NOT treat with oral antibiotics alone; CNS penetration is inadequate for meningitis.
required_recommendations: Give ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours (or cefotaxime 2 g IV every 6 hours) within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion, after blood cultures and without waiting for imaging or lumbar puncture (WHO 2025, strong recommendation; NICE NG240 1.4.1 and 1.6.3). Add vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance to penicillin or third-generation cephalosporins is highly prevalent locally (WHO 2025, conditional recommendation).
Add ampicillin 2 g IV every 4 hours for Listeria monocytogenes cover because of diabetes mellitus and the immunocompromised state (asplenia) (WHO 2025, strong recommendation; NICE NG240 1.6.6).

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3). Continue for 4 days: Streptococcus pneumoniae is identified.
Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose.

Take blood cultures and give the first dose of empirical antibiotics with dexamethasone before cranial imaging; obtain a CT head before lumbar puncture because of a severe immunocompromised state (post-traumatic asplenia with incomplete pneumococcal immunisation) (WHO 2025 section A.4); neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay treatment.
Send full CSF panel (cell count, differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, meningitis multiplex PCR, lactate) at the LP.

Narrow therapy once the organism and susceptibilities are known: stop ampicillin and continue ceftriaxone for 14 days for Streptococcus pneumoniae that is penicillin-resistant (MIC 0.12 mcg/mL) and ceftriaxone-susceptible (MIC 0.25 mcg/mL) by CLSI meningitis breakpoints, which also explains the failure of oral amoxicillin (NICE NG240).
Because of the non-blanching petechial rash, manage as possible meningococcal disease until it is excluded: droplet precautions, and notify public health if N. meningitidis is confirmed.

Recognise asplenia: after recovery complete pneumococcal conjugate vaccination (she has had PPSV23 only), meningococcal ACWY and B and Hib vaccination, and provide written asplenia advice with standby antibiotics.
Arrange formal audiological assessment before discharge, or within 4 weeks of discharge if it cannot be done before (WHO 2025, strong recommendation).

avoided_actions.rationale: ECG does not contribute to the diagnosis or acute management of bacterial meningitis.
Echocardiography is not part of the meningitis work-up; nothing in the case suggests endocarditis.
No arrhythmia indication; continuous cardiac monitoring contributes nothing to meningitis diagnosis or treatment.
PET imaging has no role in acute meningitis diagnosis; CT and MRI cover the indications.
Amyloid PET is a dementia biomarker tool with no role in acute infectious meningitis.

accepted: Acute bacterial meningitis due to Streptococcus pneumoniae, partially treated, in an asplenic patient

differential.diagnosis: Meningococcal disease (meningococcal sepsis with or without meningitis)
differential.key_features: Raised by the non-blanching petechial rash with meningism (NICE NG240 1.1.9); excluded as the cause by Neisseria meningitidis not detected on CSF PCR and Streptococcus pneumoniae isolated from 2 of 2 blood culture sets. Overwhelming pneumococcal sepsis in asplenia produces the same rash.
Excluded: neutrophilic CSF (388 cells/uL, 81% neutrophils), glucose ratio 0.19, lactate 7.6 mmol/L, Streptococcus pneumoniae on CSF PCR and in blood; viral panel targets not detected.

differential.diagnosis: Sinusitis with parameningeal spread (subdural empyema or brain abscess)

No seizures or focal deficit; HSV-1 and HSV-2 not detected on CSF PCR; neutrophilic CSF with a bacterial isolate.
Headache built up over days with fever and meningism, no thunderclap onset; no hemorrhage on CT; CSF RBC 2 cells/uL.

key_clinical_evidence: Acute bacterial meningitis presents with fever, headache, meningismus, and altered mental status; the full triad is present in only ~40%, so partial syndromes warrant aggressive workup.
Antibiotics are given within 60 minutes of suspicion; neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay them (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.4.1).

Take blood cultures and give the first dose of empirical antibiotics with dexamethasone before cranial imaging; obtain a CT head before lumbar puncture because of a severe immunocompromised state (post-traumatic asplenia with incomplete pneumococcal immunisation) (WHO 2025 section A.4); neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay treatment.

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3).

A negative Gram stain does not exclude bacterial meningitis: sensitivity is about 85% with wide confidence limits (WHO 2025), lower after antibiotics; culture and multiplex PCR establish the organism.
A CSF:blood glucose ratio of 0.4 or less is abnormally low (WHO 2025 A.2.2) and is more informative than the absolute value, above all in hyperglycemia.

Empirical therapy is ceftriaxone or cefotaxime within 60 minutes, with ampicillin when a Listeria risk factor (age over 60, pregnancy, immunocompromise) is present; vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance is locally prevalent (WHO 2025).

Asplenia (anatomic or functional) dramatically increases risk of overwhelming infection with encapsulated organisms (S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, H. influenzae); these patients require lifelong vaccination and a low threshold for empiric antibiotics.
A non-blanching petechial rash with signs of meningitis requires meningococcal disease to be strongly suspected (NICE NG240 1.1.9); in asplenia, pneumococcal sepsis can produce the same rash.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Prior antibiotics reduce Gram-stain sensitivity and can sterilise the CSF; with neutrophilic pleocytosis, a low CSF:blood glucose ratio, raised CSF lactate and a positive pneumococcal PCR, the diagnosis remains bacterial meningitis.
red_herrings.data_point: Negative CSF Gram stain in a patient with prior oral antibiotic exposure
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggest viral or aseptic meningitis and lower the threshold for withholding empiric antibiotics.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Hyponatremia is a common complication of bacterial meningitis itself (SIADH or cerebral salt wasting); assess volume status and correct it cautiously while the infection is treated. It does not point away from meningitis.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Redirect workup toward primary endocrine or volume-status causes of hyponatremia.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Prior oral antibiotic exposure attenuates the febrile response; the full clinical syndrome and CSF findings remain diagnostic.
red_herrings.data_point: Low-grade fever (38.2 C) rather than classic high fever
red_herrings.intended_effect: Reduce clinical concern for invasive bacterial infection.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The rash rightly prompts suspicion of meningococcal disease and droplet precautions (NICE NG240 1.1.9), but overwhelming pneumococcal sepsis in an asplenic patient causes the same rash; N. meningitidis not detected on CSF PCR and S. pneumoniae in 2 of 2 blood culture sets establish the organism.
red_herrings.data_point: Non-blanching petechial rash on the trunk and lower limbs
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on meningococcal disease as the final diagnosis.

sequence_constraints.reason: Under WHO 2025 section A.4 cranial imaging is not performed routinely; where readily accessible it precedes lumbar puncture when any of these is present at presentation: Glasgow Coma Score below 10, focal neurological signs, cranial nerve deficits, papilledema, new-onset seizures in adults, or a severe immunocompromised state. Here: a severe immunocompromised state (post-traumatic asplenia with incomplete pneumococcal immunisation); she is alert with GCS 14 and no focal sign. NICE NG240 does not cover this patient (asplenia) and its 1.4.7 lists no trigger here; WHO 2025 governs this benchmark. Blood cultures and the first antibiotic dose with dexamethasone come before imaging, which must not delay them.
Blood cultures are taken, and empirical antibiotics with dexamethasone given, before cranial imaging; imaging must not delay treatment (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.4.8).

clinical_pearls: Post-splenectomy patients are at lifelong risk for overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI) with encapsulated organisms, and should maintain up-to-date pneumococcal, meningococcal, and Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccinations
Prior oral antibiotic therapy can sterilise CSF cultures; multiplex PCR is critical in these scenarios
The CSF-to-blood glucose ratio is more useful than absolute CSF glucose; a ratio of 0.4 or less is abnormally low

Adjunctive dexamethasone reduced mortality in adult bacterial meningitis from 15% to 7% overall and from 34% to 14% in pneumococcal meningitis when given before or with the first antibiotic dose (de Gans & van de Beek, NEJM 2002)
A penicillin MIC of 0.12 mcg/mL is resistant by CLSI meningitis breakpoints, which explains failure of oral amoxicillin; ceftriaxone remains adequate at MIC 0.25

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Shanice Washington is a 42-year-old right-handed woman with a history of splenectomy following a motor vehicle accident at age 32, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and recurrent sinusitis who presents to the emergency department with worsening headache, confusion, and fever. Her wife provides the majority of the history as the patient is intermittently confused. She reports that approximately four days ago, she developed nasal congestion, mild headache, and a temperature of 100.2°F. She was seen by her primary care physician the following day, who diagnosed sinusitis and started amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily. For the first two days on antibiotics, her symptoms seemed to plateau — the congestion improved slightly but the headache persisted and she developed intermittent chills. Yesterday evening, her wife noticed she seemed 'not herself,' describing her as slow to answer questions and somewhat disoriented when she got up to use the bathroom, bumping into the doorframe. She attributed this to fatigue and a possible reaction to the antibiotics. This morning, she found her in bed complaining of a severe, rapidly worsening headache that she rated as 9 out of 10. She was photophobic, wincing when she opened the blinds, and when she asked her what day it was, she gave the wrong answer. She vomited once while getting dressed. Her temperature at home was 100.8°F. She immediately drove her to the emergency department, arriving at 08:45. In the ED, she reports the headache as predominantly frontal and occipital, constant, and throbbing. She denies any visual changes, weakness, or numbness in her extremities. She has no history of seizures and no witnessed seizure activity. Her wife reports she has not traveled recently, has no known sick contacts other than a student with a cold two weeks ago, and has not had any recent dental procedures. She also notes that she missed her follow-up appointment for pneumococcal vaccine booster that was recommended by her hematologist two years ago.

Marked photophobia — requests lights be dimmed. Petechial rash noted on bilateral lower extremities and trunk, approximately 15-20 scattered non-blanching petechiae 1-3 mm in size.
